what: A platform that is free to turn about a vertical axis carries one SPIKE hub, a flywheel and two opposed mass carriages. No motor drives the platform heading. Motor A turns the flywheel (vertical axis) through a 12:20 bevel pair, so 10,800 motor degrees are 6,480 flywheel degrees, or 18 turns. Motor B turns a pinion between two racks that push both masses outward together, from 32 mm to 64 mm half-spread. The program runs three cases, and each ends with both motors back where that case started: a fixed-spacing control (stages 1–2), a forward loop (stages 3–6) and the inverse loop (stages 7–10). The output is the platform’s own heading.
try: Reset, then Run. Note the platform heading at the start of each case and compare the case with its own starting heading, not with the heading at the very beginning.

Stages 1–2, the control: the flywheel turns 18 times forward and 18 times back with the masses held compact. The platform swings the opposite way by well over a full revolution, then swings back. Predict the net change before it ends.

Stages 3–6, the forward loop: compact spin forward → spread the masses (flywheel at rest) → spin back with the masses wide → pull the masses in. Is the platform’s swing during the wide reversal as large as its first swing?
Stages 7–10, the inverse loop: spread → spin forward wide → pull in → spin back compact. Before it starts, predict the sign of its net heading change compared with the forward loop.
In stages 4, 6, 7 and 9 only the masses move. Watch whether that alone turns the platform for good.
why: With the platform free in yaw and its bearing nearly frictionless, the total angular momentum about the vertical axis stays at its starting value: zero. Turning the flywheel relative to the platform therefore turns the platform backwards: J(s)·dψ + I_f·dφ = 0, so dψ = −k(s)·dφ with k(s) = I_f / J(s). J(s) is the yaw inertia of the whole machine locked together; spreading the masses raises J and lowers k. In the forward loop the platform swings by k(compact)·Φ during the compact spin but comes back only by k(wide)·Φ during the wide reversal, leaving (k(wide) − k(compact))·Φ. Moving the masses with the flywheel at rest adds nothing net, because spreading and retracting follow the same path in opposite directions. The inverse loop runs the same cycle in the opposite order, so its increment has the opposite sign. This is a geometric phase: in the ideal case the net turn depends on the loop in (spacing, flywheel angle), not on how fast it is driven. A falling cat and an astronaut use the same principle to turn without pushing on anything.
matters: Spacecraft change attitude with reaction wheels and no propellant, and changing the inertia during a wheel cycle is how a body with zero angular momentum can still end up facing a new direction. The fixed-spacing control matters as much as the loops: if it also leaves a net turn, the loop results include bearing friction, solver drift or return error, not only the shape-cycle effect.
question: Both motors end the forward loop exactly where they started. Must the platform also end at its starting heading? Which way does the inverse loop leave it?
answer: No. The compact spin swings the platform by k(compact)·Φ; the wide reversal brings it back by only k(wide)·Φ, which is smaller because the spread masses make the platform harder to turn. A net turn of (k(wide) − k(compact))·Φ remains, opposite to the flywheel’s first spin. The inverse loop runs the cycle backwards and leaves the opposite increment, in the flywheel’s forward direction. The fixed-spacing control should leave almost nothing.
further: Rough size: the supplier’s inertia estimate from the source geometry gives k ≈ 0.0892 compact and k ≈ 0.0868 wide. With Φ = 6,480° that predicts about 578° of platform swing during each flywheel leg but a net change of only about 15.4° per loop. A 2.7 % change in k, multiplied by 18 flywheel turns, is what makes the net effect visible.

Plot the platform heading against the flywheel angle relative to the platform, coloured by carriage spread. Each loop traces a thin closed shape; the two loops run round in opposite senses, and the gap between the compact and wide branches is the net turn.

Friction or damping in the yaw bearing is an outside torque and breaks the zero-momentum argument. It shows up as drift in the fixed-spacing control. Real LEGO bearings would make the net effect smaller and less repeatable.

The carriages and the flywheel use 40-tooth gears purely as ballast weights; they do not mesh with anything. In a headless Robot Lab simulation of the shipped program, measured from the platform’s pose relative to its base: k ≈ 0.0892 compact and 0.0868 wide; net yaw −14.9° for the forward loop, +15.3° for the inverse loop and −0.2° for the fixed-spacing control. That is a simulation observation, not a physical test.
formula: dψ = −k(s)·dφ with k(s) = I_f / J(s). Forward loop: Δψ = −k_c·Φ + k_w·Φ = (k_w − k_c)·Φ. Inverse loop: Δψ = (k_c − k_w)·Φ. Fixed spacing: Δψ = 0. Flywheel angle φ = 0.6 × motor A angle (12:20 bevel); carriage travel = (π/30 mm per degree) × |motor B angle|, so 305.6° of motor B ≈ 32 mm. Supplier estimate: k_c ≈ 0.0892, k_w ≈ 0.0868, Φ = 6480° → Δψ ≈ −15.4° for the forward loop.
